Authentication & Admin API\n  1421→\n  1422→### 14.1 Overview\n  1423→\n  1424→The dashboard supports **GitHub OAuth 2.0** authentication for admin operations. Public endpoints (status, health) remain unauthenticated. Admin endpoints (reboot, restart, stop/start) require login.\n  1425→\n  1426→### 14.2 Authentication Flow\n  1427→\n  1428→```\n  1429→+------------------+     +------------------+     +------------------+\n  1430→|   Dashboard UI   |     |   Flask API      |     |   GitHub OAuth   |\n  1431→+--------+---------+     +--------+---------+     +--------+---------+\n  1432→         |                        |                        |\n  1433→         | 1. Click "Login"       |                        |\n  1434→         |----------------------->|                        |\n  1435→         |                        | 2. Redirect to GitHub  |\n  1436→         |                        |----------------------->|\n  1437→         |                        |                        |\n  1438→         |                        | 3. User authorizes     |\n  1439→         |                        |<-----------------------|\n  1440→         |                        |                        |\n  1441→         | 4. Return JWT token    |                        |\n  1442→         |<-----------------------|                        |\n  1443→         |                        |                        |\n  1444→         | 5. Admin commands      |                        |\n  1445→         | (with Bearer token)    |                        |\n  1446→         |----------------------->|                        |\n  1447→         |                        |                        |\n  1448→```\n  1449→\n  1450→### 14.3 Endpoint Access Levels\n  1451→\n  1452→| Access Level | Endpoints | Auth Required |\n  1453→|--------------|-----------|---------------|\n  1454→| **Public** | `/api/health`, `/api/vms`, `/api/services`, `/api/dashboard/*` | No |\n  1455→| **Admin** | `/api/admin/vms/*/reboot`, `/api/admin/vms/*/containers/*/restart` | Yes (JWT) |\n  1456→\n  1457→### 14.4 Admin API Endpoints\n  1458→\n  1459→| Endpoint | Method | Description | Auth |\n  1460→|----------|--------|-------------|------|\n  1461→| `POST /api/auth/github` | POST | Initiate GitHub OAuth flow | No |\n  1462→| `GET /api/auth/callback` | GET | GitHub OAuth callback | No |\n  1463→| `GET /api/auth/me` | GET | Get current user info | Yes |\n  1464→| `POST /api/auth/logout` | POST | Invalidate session | Yes |\n  1465→| `POST /api/admin/vms/<id>/reboot` | POST | Reboot VM via SSH | Yes |\n  1466→| `POST /api/admin/vms/<id>/containers/<name>/restart` | POST | Restart Docker container | Yes |\n  1467→| `POST /api/admin/vms/<id>/containers/<name>/stop` | POST | Stop Docker container | Yes |\n  1468→| `POST /api/admin/vms/<id>/containers/<name>/start` | POST | Start Docker container | Yes |\n  1469→| `POST /api/admin/services/<id>/restart` | POST | Restart service (container) | Yes |\n  1470→\n  1471→### 14.5 GitHub OAuth Configuration\n  1472→\n  1473→```bash\n  1474→# Required environment variables\n  1475→GITHUB_CLIENT_ID=your_client_id\n  1476→GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET=your_client_secret\n  1477→JWT_SECRET_KEY=your_jwt_secret\n  1478→ALLOWED_GITHUB_USERS=diegonmarcos  # Comma-separated usernames\n  1479→```\n  1480→\n  1481→GitHub App settings:\n  1482→- **Authorization callback URL**: `https://cloud.diegonmarcos.com/api/auth/callback`\n  1483→- **Scopes**: `read:user` (only need username verification)\n  1484→\n  1485→### 14.6 Dashboard UI Changes\n  1486→\n  1487→**Before Login:**\n  1488→```\n  1489→+------------------------------------------+\n  1490→|  Cloud Dashboard            [Login] btn  |\n [Reboot] btn     | - [Restart] btn    |\n  1506→|  - [Containers]     | - [Stop/Start]     |\n  1507→|    - [Restart]      |                    |\n  1508→|    - [Stop/Start]   |                    |\n **Username Whitelist**: Only `ALLOWED_GITHUB_USERS` can access admin endpoints\n  1516→3. **HTTPS Only**: OAuth flow requires HTTPS\n  1517→4. **CSRF Protection**: State parameter in OAuth flow\n  1518→5. **Rate Limiting**: Admin endpoints rate-limited to prevent abuse\n  1519→6. **Audit Logging**: All admin actions logged with timestamp and user\n  1520→\n  1521→### 14.8 Implementation Status\n  1522→\n  1523→| Component | Status |\n  1524→|-----------|--------|\n  1525→| GitHub OAuth flow | `dev` |\n  1526→| JWT token generation | `dev` |\n  1527→| Admin endpoints | `dev` |\n Dashboard Architecture\n  1692→\n  1693→### 15.1 Overview\n  1694→\n  1695→The Cloud Dashboard consists of three main components:\n  1696→\n  1697→| Component | Technology | Location | Purpose |\n  1698→|-----------|------------|----------|---------|\n  1699→| **cloud-app** | HTML/CSS/JS | GitHub Pages | Static frontend UI |\n  1700→| **flask-app** | Python Flask | Oracle VM | REST API + OAuth |\n  1701→| **cloud_dash.json** | JSON | Oracle VM | Infrastructure data |\n  1702→\n  1703→### 15.2 Frontend-to-API Integration\n  1704→\n  1705→The frontend HTML fetches all data dynamically from the Flask API via JavaScript:\n  1706→\n  1707→```javascript\n  1708→// Frontend JavaScript (cloud_dash.html)\n  1709→\n  1710→// 1. Fetch VM list on page load\n  1711→async function loadVMs() {\n  1712→    const response = await fetch(\'https://cloud.diegonmarcos.com/api/vms\');\n  1713→    const vms = await response.json();\n  1714→    renderVMTable(vms);\n  1715→}\n  1716→\n  1717→// 2. Fetch live status for each VM\n  1718→async function checkVMStatus(vmId) {\n  1719→    const response = await fetch(`https://cloud.diegonmarcos.com/api/vms/${vmId}/status`);\n  1720→    const status = await response.json();\n  1721→    updateStatusIndicator(vmId, status);\n  1722→}\n  1723→\n  1724→// 3. Admin actions (requires OAuth token)\n  1725→async function rebootVM(vmId) {\n  1726→    const token = localStorage.getItem(\'github_token\');\n  1727→    const response = await fetch(`https://cloud.diegonmarcos.com/api/vm/${vmId}/reboot`, {\n  1728→        method: \'POST\',\n  1729→        headers: { \'Authorization\': `Bearer ${token}` }\n  1730→    });\n  1731→    return response.json();\n  1732→}\n  1733→```\n  1734→\n  1735→### 15.3 API Endpoint → Frontend Mapping\n  1736→\n  1737→| Frontend Feature | API Endpoint | Data Used |\n  1738→|------------------|--------------|-----------|\n  1739→| VM Table | `GET /api/vms` | name, IP, status, services |\n  1740→| VM Status Indicators | `GET /api/vms/<id>/status` | ping, ssh, uptime |\n  1741→| Service Cards | `GET /api/services` | name, URL, status |\n  1742→| Service Health | `GET /api/services/<id>/status` | http_check, response_time |\n  1743→| Reboot Button | `POST /api/vm/<id>/reboot` | success/error message |\n  1744→| Login State | `GET /api/auth/me` | username, avatar |\n  1745→\n  1746→### 15.4 Architecture Visualization Pages\n  1747→\n  1748→The dashboard includes pages that render Mermaid diagrams from the spec files:\n  1749→\n  1750→| Page | Source | Content |\n  1751→|------|--------|---------|\n  1752→| `arch.html` | Cloud-spec_Tables.md (Mermaid) | Infrastructure tree diagram |\n  1753→| `ai-arch.html` | Cloud-spec_Tables.md (Mermaid) | AI services architecture |\n  1754→\n  1755→**Rendering Process:**\n  1756→1. Mermaid code is authored in `Cloud-spec_Tables.md` (source of truth)\n  1757→2. HTML pages include Mermaid.js library\n  1758→3. Mermaid code is embedded in `<pre class="mermaid">` blocks\n  1759→4. Mermaid.js renders SVG diagrams at runtime\n  1760→\n  1761→---\n  1762→\n  1763→## 16. You need to **turn OFF** DNSSEC before changing nameservers.

## Steps:

1. **Disable DNSSEC** - Toggle that switch OFF
   - It says "DNS Security Extensions" - turn it OFF
   - This is required because Cloudflare will manage DNSSEC after migration

2. **Wait a few minutes** for DNSSEC to deactivate

3. **Then change nameservers** to:
   ```
   burt.ns.cloudflare.com
   phoenix.ns.cloudflare.com
   ```

**Note about Google Workspace:**
Your domain uses Google Workspace for email/services. This is fine - Cloudflare will just manage DNS. Your Google Workspace (Gmail, etc.) will continue working. Cloudflare will import the existing MX records pointing to Google.

After Cloudflare is active, you can:
- Keep Google Workspace working (existing MX records)
- Add Cloudflare Email Routing alongside it
- Or fully migrate to Stalwart later

Turn off DNSSEC first, then proceed with nameserver change.

ASSISTANT (line 4722):
----------------------------------------
**No, it's not a problem.** DNSSEC is separate from Google Workspace functionality.

| What | Impact |
|------|--------|
| **DNSSEC OFF** | No impact on services, just less DNS security (temporary) |
| **Google Workspace** | Will continue working - uses MX records, not DNSSEC |
| **Gmail, Calendar, Drive** | All keep working |

**What happens:**

1. Turn OFF DNSSEC at Google/Squarespace
2. Change nameservers to Cloudflare
3. Cloudflare imports all your DNS records (including Google Workspace MX records)
4. Google Workspace keeps working (Gmail, etc.)
5. You can re-enable DNSSEC **in Cloudflare** later (free)

The "managed by Google Workspace" warning is just telling you the domain is linked to Workspace - it doesn't mean you can't change DNS providers.

**Safe to proceed.** Turn off DNSSEC and change nameservers.

No, **Stalwart doesn't include webmail**. It's just the mail server (IMAP/SMTP/JMAP backend).

**Options for webmail:**

| Webmail | RAM | Notes |
|---------|-----|-------|
| **Roundcube** | ~50MB | Classic, PHP-based |
| **Snappymail** | ~30MB | Lightweight, fast |
| **SOGo** | ~200MB | Full groupware (calendar, contacts) |
| **Cypht** | ~20MB | Minimal, aggregator |

**Quickest option** - Deploy Roundcube or Snappymail on the same VM:

```bash
# Snappymail (lightest)
docker run -d --name snappymail \
  -p 8888:8888 \
  -e MEMORY_LIMIT=128M \
  djmaze/snappymail
```

Then configure it to connect to Stalwart IMAP on `localhost:993`.

**Snappymail vs Cypht**

| Feature | Snappymail | Cypht |
|---------|------------|-------|
| **RAM** | ~30-50MB | ~20-30MB |
| **Docker Image** | ~100MB | ~50MB |
| **UI** | Modern, Gmail-like | Minimal, modular |
| **Speed** | Fast | Very fast |
| **IMAP Support** | Full | Full |
| **Multiple Accounts** | Yes | Yes (aggregator) |
| **Contacts** | Yes | Basic |
| **Calendar** | No | No |
| **Search** | Good | Basic |
| **Mobile** | Responsive | Responsive |
| **Setup** | Easy | Easy |
| **Active Development** | Very active | Moderate |

**Visual Comparison:**

```
Snappymail:                          Cypht:
┌─────────────────────────┐          ┌─────────────────────────┐
│ ☰ │ Inbox (12)    │ ⚙  │          │ Combined │ Gmail │ Work │
├───┼────────────────────┤          ├─────────────────────────┤
│ 📥│ • Email 1          │          │ • Email 1 (Gmail)       │
│ 📤│ • Email 2          │          │ • Email 2 (Work)        │
│ 📝│ • Email 3          │          │ • Email 3 (Gmail)       │
│ 🗑│                    │          │                         │
└───┴────────────────────┘          └─────────────────────────┘
  Gmail-like interface                 Feed/aggregator style
```

**Recommendation:**
- **Snappymail** → Better UX, more features, feels like a real email client
- **Cypht** → Lighter, good if you aggregate multiple accounts

**For single Stalwart account: Snappymail** is better.

ASSISTANT (line 6267):

No, emails won't be immediately lost. Here's how SMTP works:

## Email Delivery Resilience

**SMTP retry mechanism**: When a sending server can't deliver to your server, it **queues the email and retries** for 3-7 days (depending on the sender's configuration). Most mail servers retry every 15-60 minutes.

## Your Current Setup (Cloudflare → Stalwart)

```
Sender → Cloudflare MX → Worker → Stalwart (down?)
                              ↘ Gmail (backup copy)
```

If Stalwart is down:
- The Worker's `fetch()` to Stalwart fails
- Gmail forward still works (independent)
- You get the email in Gmail, just not in Stalwart

## Options for High Availability

| Option | How it works |
|--------|-------------|
| **Gmail as backup** | Forward to Gmail first, sync to Stalwart later (what you have) |
| **Multiple MX** | Add Gmail MX as lower priority backup |
| **Cloudflare queuing** | Cloudflare Email Routing buffers briefly on failure |

## Recommended Architecture

```
Internet → Cloudflare MX
              ↓
         Gmail (primary storage, always up)
              ↓
         Sync script → Stalwart (your server)
```

This way:
- Gmail is always available (99.99% uptime)
- Stalwart syncs when online
- No email loss if your VPS goes down

The sync script in `/tmp/gmail_to_stalwart_sync.py` does exactly this - pulls from Gmail IMAP into Stalwart. Want me to set it up as a cron job on the VPS?

**ROOT CAUSE FOUND:**

Your **router (192.168.1.1)** is the DNS server for your system, and **your router cannot resolve `mail.diegonmarcos.com`**.

| DNS Server | Query Result |
|------------|--------------|
| Your router (192.168.1.1) | **EMPTY** (fails) |
| Google DNS (8.8.8.8) | `130.110.251.193` (works) |
| Cloudflare DNS (1.1.1.1) | `130.110.251.193` (works) |

**Why your router fails to resolve:**

1. **ISP DNS filtering** - Your router forwards DNS to your ISP, which may filter/block certain domains
2. **DNS rebind protection** - Some routers block domains resolving to "unusual" IPs as a security measure
3. **Stale cache** - Your router may have cached a failed lookup
4. **Router DNS configuration** - Your router's upstream DNS servers may not have propagated the record

**Solution: Configure your system to use public DNS directly:**

I need sudo password. Here's what you need to run manually to fix DNS:

```bash
# Create DNS override config
sudo mkdir -p /etc/systemd/resolved.conf.d
sudo tee /etc/systemd/resolved.conf.d/dns.conf << 'EOF'
[Resolve]
DNS=8.8.8.8 1.1.1.1
FallbackDNS=8.8.4.4 1.0.0.1
EOF

# Restart systemd-resolved
sudo systemctl restart systemd-resolved

# Verify fix
dig mail.diegonmarcos.com +short
```

**Summary - The Reason:**

Your system → asks `127.0.0.53` (systemd-resolved) → asks `192.168.1.1` (your router) → **router returns EMPTY**

Your router's DNS (likely your ISP's DNS) is not resolving `mail.diegonmarcos.com`. This is common with ISP DNS servers - they may have stale caches, filtering, or simply slower propagation.

After running those commands, your system will use Google (8.8.8.8) and Cloudflare (1.1.1.1) DNS directly, bypassing your router's broken DNS.

## Your Architecture vs NextCloud Comparison

### Current Architecture RAM Summary

| VM | RAM | Services | Usage |
|----|-----|----------|-------|
| oci-f-micro_1 | 1 GB | Mail (Stalwart) | ~520 MB |
| oci-f-micro_2 | 1 GB | Matomo | ~512 MB |
| gcp-f-micro_1 | 1 GB | NPM proxy | ~200 MB |
| oci-p-flex_1 | 8 GB | n8n, Syncthing, Git, Dashboard, VPN, Terminal | ~1-2 GB (wake-on-demand) |
| **Total Active** | **3 GB** | | **~1.2-1.5 GB** |

---

### NextCloud Requirements

| Config | RAM | Storage | Notes |
|--------|-----|---------|-------|
| Bare minimum | 512 MB | 10 GB | Unusable in practice |
| Basic (1-5 users) | **2-4 GB** | 50 GB | Slow, timeouts on large files |
| Production | **4-8 GB** | 100+ GB | Recommended for single user |
| Heavy use | 16+ GB | 500+ GB | With Office, Talk, etc. |

**NextCloud components:**
```
NextCloud Stack (monolithic):
├── PHP-FPM          (~300-800 MB)
├── MySQL/MariaDB    (~500-1000 MB)
├── Redis            (~64-256 MB)
├── Nginx/Apache     (~100-200 MB)
├── Cron jobs        (~50-100 MB spikes)
└── Background tasks (~variable)
Total: ~1.5-3 GB just to run
```

---

### Side-by-Side Comparison

| Aspect | Your Architecture | NextCloud |
|--------|------------------|-----------|
| **RAM (idle)** | ~800 MB-1.5 GB | ~1.5-3 GB |
| **RAM (active)** | ~2-3 GB | ~3-6 GB |
| **Min viable VM** | 1 GB (distributed) | 4 GB (single) |
| **Storage overhead** | Low (purpose-built) | High (PHP, many deps) |
| **Startup time** | Fast (containers) | Slow (PHP boot) |
| **Updates** | Per-service | All-or-nothing |
| **Failure blast radius** | Single service | Everything |
| **Customization** | Full control | Plugin-limited |

---

### What You'd Lose with NextCloud

| Your Service | NextCloud Equivalent | Quality |
|--------------|---------------------|---------|
| **Syncthing** | NextCloud Files | Worse - web-first, not P2P |
| **Stalwart Mail** | None (client only) | **No server** - need external |
| **Matomo** | None | **No equivalent** |
| **n8n** | NextCloud Flow (basic) | Much worse - limited automation |
| **Gitea** | None | **No equivalent** |
| **Custom Dashboard** | None | **No equivalent** |
| **Web Terminal** | None | **No equivalent** |

---

### What You'd Gain with NextCloud

| Feature | Your Current | NextCloud |
|---------|--------------|-----------|
| Calendar/Contacts | None | CalDAV/CardDAV built-in |
| Office suite | None | Collabora/OnlyOffice |
| Video calls | None | NextCloud Talk |
| Notes | None | Built-in |
| Photo gallery | Planned (PhotoView) | Built-in |
| Mobile apps | Syncthing only | Full sync + office |

---

### Migration Impact

**If you switched to NextCloud:**

```
BEFORE (distributed):                    AFTER (NextCloud):
┌─────────────────────────────────┐     ┌─────────────────────────────────┐

## Lightweight Self-Hosted Alternatives

### Calendar/Contacts (CalDAV/CardDAV)

| Solution | RAM | Storage | Notes |
|----------|-----|---------|-------|
| **Baikal** | ~30-50 MB | ~50 MB | PHP, simplest, battle-tested |
| **Radicale** | ~20-40 MB | ~30 MB | Python, single-file config, lightest |
| **DAViCal** | ~100-200 MB | ~100 MB | PostgreSQL backend, more features |

**Recommendation:** **Radicale** - fits a 1GB VM, single binary, no database needed.

```yaml
# docker-compose.yml - Radicale
radicale:
  image: tomsquest/docker-radicale
  container_name: radicale
  ports:
    - "127.0.0.1:5232:5232"
  volumes:
    - ./data:/data
  restart: unless-stopped
```

---

### Office Suite (Self-Hosted)

| Solution | RAM | Type | Notes |
|----------|-----|------|-------|
| **OnlyOffice Docs** | ~2-4 GB | Full suite | Word/Excel/PPT, best MS Office compat |
| **Collabora Online** | ~1-2 GB | LibreOffice-based | Good compatibility, lighter |
| **CryptPad** | ~512 MB-1 GB | Encrypted, no accounts needed | Unique - E2E encrypted, collaborative |

**For your setup:**

| If you need... | Choose | Deploy on |
|----------------|--------|-----------|
| MS Office compatibility | OnlyOffice | oci-f-arm_1 (24GB) |
| Lighter, occasional use | Collabora | oci-p-flex_1 (8GB) |
| Privacy-first, simple | **CryptPad** | oci-f-micro (1GB edge case) |

**Recommendation:** **CryptPad** - runs on ~500MB, E2E encrypted, no user management needed:

```yaml
# docker-compose.yml - CryptPad
cryptpad:
  image: cryptpad/cryptpad:latest
  container_name: cryptpad
  ports:
    - "127.0.0.1:3000:3000"
  volumes:
    - ./data/blob:/cryptpad/blob
    - ./data/block:/cryptpad/block
    - ./data/data:/cryptpad/data
    - ./data/files:/cryptpad/datastore
  environment:
    - CPAD_MAIN_DOMAIN=https://pad.diegonmarcos.com
  restart: unless-stopped
```

---

### Summary for Your Spec

| Service | Solution | RAM | VM Target |
|---------|----------|-----|-----------|
| Calendar/Contacts | Radicale | 30 MB | oci-f-micro_1 or oci-p-flex_1 |
| Office Suite | CryptPad | 500 MB | oci-p-flex_1 (wake-on-demand) |

Both fit your microservices philosophy - purpose-built, lightweight, no bloat.

ASSISTANT (line 7640):

The certificate chain is valid and verification passes. The issue is likely that your mobile app is configured to connect to the **IP address** (130.110.251.193) instead of the **hostname** (mail.diegonmarcos.com).

The SSL certificate is issued for `mail.diegonmarcos.com`, so:
- If you connect using `mail.diegonmarcos.com` → certificate is trusted
- If you connect using `130.110.251.193` → certificate doesn't match, so it's "untrusted"

**Fix**: In your mobile email app settings, make sure you're using:
- **IMAP Server**: `mail.diegonmarcos.com` (not the IP)
- **SMTP Server**: `mail.diegonmarcos.com` (not the IP)
- **Port IMAP**: 993 (SSL/TLS)
- **Port SMTP**: 465 (SSL/TLS)

ASSISTANT (line 7654):
----------------------------------------
For Samsung mail app, use these settings:

**IMAP (Incoming mail):**
- Server: `mail.diegonmarcos.com`
- Port: `993`
- Security: **SSL**

**SMTP (Outgoing mail):**
- Server: `mail.diegonmarcos.com`
- Port: `587`
- Security: **TLS** (this is STARTTLS)

The difference:
- **SSL** (port 993/465) = Connection is encrypted from the start
- **TLS** (port 587) = Connection starts unencrypted, then upgrades to encrypted (STARTTLS)

Both are secure, just different methods. Port 587 with TLS is the modern standard for SMTP submission.

ASSISTANT (line 7835):

Yes, **blocked by default on ALL tenancies** created after June 2021 (including paid). But you can **request an exemption**:

## Options:

1. **Request Port 25 Unblock** (Paid accounts only)
   - Go to OCI Console → Help → Service Limits Request
   - Request exemption for outbound port 25
   - Takes a few days to process

2. **Use Oracle Email Delivery Service** (Free tier available)
   - Oracle's own SMTP relay service
   - Bypass port 25 block entirely
   - Configure Stalwart to relay through it

3. **Use external relay** (Brevo, SendGrid, etc.)
   - Connects on port 587 (not blocked)
   - Simplest solution

Since you're on the free tier, option 2 or 3 is your path. Would you like me to help set up **Oracle Email Delivery** (free) or an external relay?

The security list rule for port 25 is correctly configured, but **Oracle Cloud blocks port 25 at the infrastructure level** - this is separate from the Security List.

**Summary of the situation:**

| Direction | Status | Solution |
|-----------|--------|----------|
| **Inbound Port 25** | Blocked by Oracle infrastructure | Keep using Cloudflare Workers/Email Routing |
| **Outbound Port 25** | Blocked by Oracle infrastructure | Use SMTP relay (Oracle Email Delivery) |

Oracle Cloud blocks port 25 (both in and out) for tenancies created after June 2021 to prevent spam. This can only be unblocked by:
1. Submitting a support ticket to Oracle
2. Requires a **paid support plan** (not available on free tier)

**Your current architecture must remain:**

```
INBOUND:  Internet → Cloudflare Email Routing → Worker → Stalwart (via 587/HTTPS)
OUTBOUND: Stalwart → Oracle Email Delivery relay → Internet
```

The Cloudflare Workers approach already bypasses the port 25 block for inbound since it uses HTTPS/LMTP to deliver to your server.

When a message is processed for delivery, the selected routing strategy defines whether it should be delivered locally, resolved through DNS, or sent through an intermediate relay server.(no content)There are three types of routing strategies supported:\n- **Local**: Delivers the message to the local message store, typically for users hosted on the same system or domain\n- **MX**: Uses DNS MX record resolution to determine the destination server for remote delivery\n- **Relay**: Forwards the message to a predefined relay host, regardless of recipient domain\n\n### Configuration\n\nRouting strategies are defined in the configuration under the `queue.route.<id>` section, where `<id>` is the name of the routing strategy. The type of routing to use is specified using the `queue.route.<id>.type` setting, which must be one of the following: local, mx, or relay.\n\n### Setting Up a Relay (Next-Hop)\n\nTo configure Stalwart to use a relay for external mails, go to Settings -> SMTP -> Outbound -> Routing. Add the relay as the next hop. When using relays you have to disable DANE and MTA-STS.(no content)In Settings -> SMTP -> Outbound -> TLS change them to disabled.\n\n### Example NixOS Configuration\n\nFor a minimal configuration, you can set `queue.outbound.next-hop = "\'local\'"` to route messages locally.\n\n### Relay Host Use Cases\n\nThe relay routing strategy is used to deliver messages through a predefined relay host instead of sending them directly to the recipient\'s domain via MX resolution. A relay host is a server that accepts email from another server and then forwards it to its final destination. The server that accepts and forwards the emails is known as a relay because it functions as an intermediate stop for messages on their way to their final destination.(no content)Some organizations might not want to handle the complexity of direct delivery, so they send all their outgoing mail to a relay host (like an Internet Service Provider\'s mail server) which handles the details of delivery. Another common usage scenario is when sending emails from a network that\'s behind a firewall or when the server IP is on a blocklist.\n\n### Known Issues\n\nUsers have reported issues when setting up an SMTP relay behind a CGNAT - doing so can break the ability to receive inbound email.\n\nFor the official documentation, you can visit the Stalwart Labs routing documentation at **stalw.art/docs/mta/outbound/routing/**.\n\n\nREMINDER: You MUST include the sources above in your response to the user using markdown hyperlinks.'}]

The type of routing to use is specified using the `queue.route.<id>.type` setting, which must be one of the following: `local`, `mx`, or `relay`.\n\n### Routing Types\n\nThere are three types of routing strategies supported:\n- **Local**: Delivers the message to the local message store, typically for users hosted on the same system or domain\n- **MX**: Uses DNS MX record resolution to determine the destination server for remote delivery\n- **Relay**: Forwards the message to a predefined relay host, regardless of recipient domain\n\n### Relay Routing Strategy\n\nThe relay routing strategy is used to deliver messages through a predefined relay host instead of sending them directly to the recipient\'s domain via MX resolution. A relay host is a server that accepts email from another server and then forwards it to its final destination.(no content)Some organizations might not want to handle the complexity of direct delivery, so they send all their outgoing mail to a relay host (like an Internet Service Provider\'s mail server). Another common usage scenario is when sending emails from a network that\'s behind a firewall or when the server IP is on a blocklist.\n\n## Configuration via Web Panel\n\nGo to Settings -> SMTP -> Outbound -> Routing. Add the relay as the next hop. When using relays you have to disable DANE and MTA-STS.(no content)When using relays you have to disable DANE and MTA-STS. However doing so appears to break my ability to receive any inbound email."(no content)If you encounter "Relay not allowed" errors, it may indicate you have not properly configured a local domain. ## Summary: Stalwart Mail Server OCI Email Delivery Relay - WORKING

The outbound email relay via Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) Email Delivery is now **fully operational**.

### Configuration Details

**Stalwart Config** (`/opt/stalwart/etc/config.toml`):
```toml
[queue.route."oci-relay"]
type = "relay"
address = "smtp.email.eu-marseille-1.oci.oraclecloud.com"
port = 587
protocol = "smtp"

[queue.route."oci-relay".tls]
implicit = false
allow-invalid-certs = false

[queue.route."oci-relay".auth]
username = "ocid1.user.oc1...<truncated>@...xr.com"
secret = "H;OR3xZ-F:}u#Cd2!Z>9"

[queue.outbound]
next-hop = "'oci-relay'"

[queue.outbound.limits]
dane = "disable"
mta-sts = "disable"

[queue.strategy]
route = "'oci-relay'"
```

### Test Results
- **Email queued**: `Message queued with id 3de03ccfca00138`
- **Relayed via**: `smtp.email.eu-marseille-1.oci.oraclecloud.com:587`
- **TLS**: `TLSv1_2` with `TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256`
- **Status**: `250 Ok` - Message delivered successfully

### Key Points
1. **Authenticated submission required**: Port 587 with STARTTLS and user authentication is needed for sending outbound mail
2. **Relay routes external mail**: All external recipients are routed through OCI Email Delivery
3. **Local delivery works**: Inbound emails to `me@diegonmarcos.com` are delivered locally
4. **Port 25 blocked**: Oracle Cloud blocks outbound port 25, which is why the relay is essential

The email should arrive at `diegonmarcos@live.com` shortly. You can check your Outlook inbox.

The type of routing to use is specified using the `queue.route.<id>.type` setting, which must be one of the following: `local`, `mx`, or `relay`.\n\n### Relay Route Setup\nThe relay routing strategy is used to deliver messages through a predefined relay host instead of sending them directly to the recipient\'s domain via MX resolution. A relay host is a server that accepts email from another server and then forwards it to its final destination. The server that accepts and forwards the emails is known as a relay because it functions as an intermediate stop for messages on their way to their final destination.\n\n### Configuration Parameters\nFor each remote host, the following parameters can be specified as sub-keys of `route.<id>`: `address`: The fully-qualified domain name of the remote server, for example "mail.domain.org". `port`: The port on the remote server that should be used for the connection. `protocol`: The communication protocol to use, with valid options being `lmtp` or `smtp`.\n\n### Next-Hop Configuration Example\nA configuration example shows how to set up conditional routing:\n```\n[queue.outbound]\nnext-hop = [ { if = "rcpt_domain == \'stalwart.mx.domain\'", then = "\'local\'" }, { else = false } ]\n```\n\n### Using External Relays\nTo configure Stalwart to use a relay for external mails: Go to Settings -> SMTP -> Outbound -> Routing. Add the relay as the next hop. When using relays you have to disable DANE and MTA-STS.\n\n### NixOS Configuration Example\nThe NixOS Wiki shows a configuration example where `queue.outbound.next-hop = "\'local\'"` is set to route all outbound messages locally.\n\n### Important Notes\nWhen encountering "Relay not allowed" errors, it may indicate that you have not properly configured a local domain. Perhaps the lookup query to resolve local domains is not working. When a message is processed for delivery, the selected routing strategy defines whether it should be delivered locally, resolved through DNS, or sent through an intermediate relay server. There are three types of routing strategies supported: Local (delivers the message to the local message store), MX (uses DNS MX record resolution to determine the destination server for remote delivery), and Relay (forwards the message to a predefined relay host, regardless of recipient domain).\n\n### Configuration Location\nRouting strategies are defined in the configuration under the `queue.route.<id>` section, where `<id>` is the name of the routing strategy. The type of routing to use is specified using the `queue.route.<id>.type` setting, which must be one of the following: local, mx, or relay.\n\n### Setting Up a Relay (Next-Hop)\nTo configure Stalwart to use a relay for external mails, go to Settings -> SMTP -> Outbound -> Routing. Add your relay service (e.g., smtp2go) as the next hop. When using relays you have to disable DANE and MTA-STS.(no content)In Settings -> SMTP -> Outbound -> TLS, change DANE and MTA-STS to disabled.\n\n### NixOS Configuration Example\nFor NixOS users, the next-hop can be configured with `queue.outbound.next-hop = "\'local\'"` in the settings block.\n\n### Relay Host Usage\nThe relay routing strategy is used to deliver messages through a predefined relay host instead of sending them directly to the recipient\'s domain via MX resolution. A relay host is a server that accepts email from another server and then forwards it to its final destination.(no content)Some organizations might not want to handle the complexity of direct delivery, so they send all their outgoing mail to a relay host which handles the details of delivery. Another common usage scenario is when sending emails from a network that\'s behind a firewall or when the server IP is on a blocklist.\n\n### Common Issues\nThe directory is first checked for local domains and addresses and if they can\'t be found then the "Allow Relaying" expressions are evaluated.\n\nFor more detailed documentation, visit the official Stalwart documentation at [stalw.art/docs/mta/outbound/routing/](https://stalw.art/docs/mta/outbound/routing/).\n\n\nREMINDER: You MUST include the sources above in your response to the user using markdown hyperlinks.'}]

This allows, for example, some messages to be delivered locally while others are relayed or sent via MX resolution based on domain, authentication status, or other delivery context.\n\n### Relay Routing Strategy\n\nThe relay routing strategy is used to deliver messages through a predefined relay host instead of sending them directly to the recipient\'s domain via MX resolution. A relay host is a server that accepts email from another server and then forwards it to its final destination. The server that accepts and forwards the emails is known as a relay because it functions as an intermediate stop for messages on their way to their final destination.(no content)Some organizations might not want to handle the complexity of direct delivery, so they send all their outgoing mail to a relay host (like an Internet Service Provider\'s mail server) which handles the details of delivery. Another common usage scenario is when sending emails from a network that\'s behind a firewall or when the server IP is on a blocklist.\n\n### Configuration Parameters\n\n- **protocol**: The communication protocol to use, with valid options being `lmtp` or `smtp`.\n- **TLS settings** under `route.<id>.tls`: `implicit` specifies whether TLS should be implicitly established upon connecting or negotiated via STARTTLS (defaults to true). `allow-invalid-certs` indicates whether self-signed and invalid certificates should be accepted (defaults to false).\n- **Authentication** under `route.<id>.auth`: `username` for authentication, and `secret` for the password. Queue is now empty. **OCI Email Delivery relay is fully working!**

## Summary: OCI Email Relay Fix

### What was wrong:
1. **Wrong config key**: Was using `queue.outbound.next-hop` instead of `queue.strategy.route`
2. **Expression parsing error**: Value `oci-relay` was parsed as expression (oci minus relay) instead of literal string
3. **Quote escaping**: Single quotes `'oci-relay'` were being stripped by shell

### The fix:
Used Python subprocess to set the configuration with preserved single quotes:
```python
subprocess.run([..., "server", "add-config", "queue.strategy.route", "'oci-relay'"])
```

### Working configuration:
```
queue.strategy.route = 'oci-relay'
queue.route.oci-relay.type = relay
queue.route.oci-relay.address = smtp.email.eu-marseille-1.oci.oraclecloud.com
queue.route.oci-relay.port = 587
queue.route.oci-relay.protocol = smtp
queue.route.oci-relay.tls.implicit = false
queue.route.oci-relay.auth.username = (OCI SMTP user)
queue.route.oci-relay.auth.secret = (password)
```

### Verified working:
```
✓ Email sent from me@diegonmarcos.com to diegonmarcos@outlook.com
✓ Connected to smtp.email.eu-marseille-1.oci.oraclecloud.com:587
✓ STARTTLS TLSv1_2
✓ Message delivered (code 250, "Ok")
✓ Queue empty
```

**The test email "OCI Relay Test - 04:25:48" should be in your Outlook inbox now.** You can also test sending from Thunderbird - it should work through the OCI relay.

Here's a comparison of self-hosted email servers with RAM usage and features:

## Email Server Comparison

| Server | RAM Usage | Docker | SMTP Relay Config | Learning Curve | Features |
|--------|-----------|--------|-------------------|----------------|----------|
| **Stalwart** | ~100-200MB | ✅ | Complex (toml/db hybrid) | High | All-in-one, Rust, JMAP, IMAP, POP3, CalDAV/CardDAV, built-in webadmin |
| **docker-mailserver** | ~200-400MB | ✅ | Simple (env vars) | Low | Postfix+Dovecot, battle-tested, great docs, SpamAssassin, ClamAV |
| **Mailcow** | ~1-2GB | ✅ | Medium (UI) | Medium | Full-featured, SOGo webmail, rspamd, nice UI, resource heavy |
| **Mailu** | ~400-800MB | ✅ | Simple (env) | Low | Lightweight, webmail, antispam, good for small setups |
| **Maddy** | ~50-100MB | ✅ | Simple (config) | Low | Go, minimal, single binary, no webmail |
| **Postal** | ~500MB | ✅ | Simple (rails) | Medium | Designed for sending, good for transactional mail |
| **iRedMail** | ~500MB-1GB | ⚠️ Script | Medium (postfix) | Medium | Traditional, OpenLDAP/MySQL, web admin |

## Recommendations for OCI Relay

**Best for your case (simple relay):**

1. **docker-mailserver** - Relay config is just:
   ```env
   RELAY_HOST=smtp.email.eu-marseille-1.oci.oraclecloud.com
   RELAY_PORT=587
   RELAY_USER=ocid1.user...
   RELAY_PASSWORD=your-password
   ```

2. **Maddy** - Ultra lightweight, simple config:
   ```
   smtp tcp://0.0.0.0:587 {
     deliver_to &remote_queue
   }
   target.queue remote_queue {
     target smtp://smtp.email.eu-marseille-1.oci.oraclecloud.com:587 {
       auth plain <username> <password>
     }
   }
   ```

Which one do you want to try? I recommend **docker-mailserver** - it's the most battle-tested with the simplest relay configuration.

----------------------------------------
## Mobile Client Authentication

**Short answer:** Neither Snappymail nor Stalwart provide 2FA for mobile email clients.

### How it works:

```
Mobile App (iOS/Android Mail, Outlook, Thunderbird)
         │
         │ IMAP/SMTP (username + password only)
         ▼
    ┌─────────────┐
    │  Stalwart   │  ← Handles IMAP/SMTP auth (NO 2FA possible)
    │  Mail Server│
    └─────────────┘

Browser (Webmail)
         │
         │ HTTPS
         ▼
    ┌─────────────┐
    │  Snappymail │  ← Can have 2FA plugin for web login
    │  (Webmail)  │
    └─────────────┘
         │
         │ IMAP/SMTP
         ▼
    ┌─────────────┐
    │  Stalwart   │
    └─────────────┘
```

### The Problem

| Access Method | 2FA Possible? | Why |
|--------------|---------------|-----|
| Admin Panel (Stalwart) | ✅ Yes | Web interface |
| Webmail (Snappymail) | ✅ Yes (plugin) | Web interface |
| Mobile/Desktop IMAP/SMTP | ❌ No | Protocol limitation |

**IMAP/SMTP protocols don't support 2FA** - they only use username + password.

### Solutions for Mobile 2FA

| Solution | How it works |
|----------|--------------|
| **App Passwords** | Generate unique passwords per device (Gmail-style) |
| **OAuth2** | Delegate auth to identity provider |
| **Client Certificates** | Install cert on device |

**Servers with App Passwords:**
- Mailcow ✅
- Mailu ✅ (via web UI)
- Stalwart ❌
- Modoboa ✅

If you need 2FA protection for mobile access, **Mailu** or **Mailcow** with App Passwords is the way to go.
